dish: omakase sushi, kaiseki tasting, chirashi
w: The city's benchmark for traditional Japanese dining: a MICHELIN-starred kaiseki-and-sushi room above a Dupont Circle CVS, run by second-generation chef Nobu Yamazaki, who reinvented the family restaurant into an upmarket kaiseki house. The MICHELIN star is a lone institutional authority; Time Out ranks it among DC's very best Japanese. Fish is flown from Toyosu.

dish: Beijing duck, mapo tofu, dan dan noodles, walnut prawns
w: Sichuan legend Peter Chang's polished DC flagship, where he applies precision to Sichuan and classic Chinese cooking without dialing down the heat. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema reviewed it as "worth the wait," Esquire named it a Best New Restaurant (2023), and it carries a MICHELIN Guide listing; The Infatuation is a fan. Peter Chang is a past James Beard finalist.

dish: cassava cake with crab fat, ube bao sliders, lechon
w: Chef Paolo Dungca's modern Filipino restaurant, reborn in a casual Dupont Circle storefront in August 2025 after leaving H Street. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (2026) and reviewed by the Washington Post's Tom Sietsema as "a boundless vision of Filipino cooking"; the signature savory cassava cake with crab fat, jamón and trout roe carried over from the tasting-menu original.

dish: khao soi, funky fruit-and-curry stews, larb, papaya salad
w: Chef Jeeraporn Poksupthong's Northern Thai kitchen in Mount Vernon Triangle (the successor to Baan Thai) turns out exemplary khao soi and funky fruit-filled curried stews. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants and to the New York Times' "25 Best Restaurants in Washington, DC, Right Now"; The Infatuation calls it a standout.

dish: Sapporo-style ramen, izakaya small plates
w: The restaurant that introduced DC to serious ramen (2013): a Sapporo-style ramen bar downstairs with noodles handcrafted and imported from Japan, and a full izakaya upstairs, from chef Katsuya Fukushima. A perennial Eater essential; The Infatuation and Gayot both rate it a Chinatown/Penn Quarter must, and there's usually a line.

dish: ceviche, lomo saltado (chifa), Nikkei tiraditos, pisco sours
w: José Andrés's Penn Quarter homage to Peru's three tables — criollo, Chifa (Chinese-Peruvian) and Nikkei (Japanese-Peruvian) — with the country's largest pisco collection. Washington City Paper and Washingtonian covered its debut; it held a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand (2017–2020) and just marked its 10th anniversary. A rare deep dive into authentic chifa/Nikkei rather than generic "Latin."

dish: jollof rice, egusi, bitterleaf soup, beef suya, Lagos snapper
w: DC's upscale West African flagship (opened 2024) from Nigerian-American founder Ope Amosu, a 175-seat downtown room built around a Nigerian core — egusi, bitterleaf (ofe onugbu), beef suya, Lagos snapper — that shifts to a lounge scene on weekends. Reviewed by The Infatuation and featured in Destination DC's dining coverage; fills a real West African gap for a "Chocolate City."

dish: seasonal sashimi, scallop carpaccio, crab-and-corn croquettes
w: A compact two-story father-daughter izakaya a block off U Street, sourcing fish from Tokyo's Toyosu market and rotating sashimi with the seasons. The Washington Post's Elazar Sontag made it his first four-star review (2026), calling it a triumph of Japanese comfort cooking; Time Out lists it among DC's best. Understated, precise, extraordinary.

dish: kare-kare, lechon kawali, lumpia, ube desserts
address: 3155 Mount Pleasant St NW, Washington, DC 20010
w: Patrice Cleary's warm Mount Pleasant Filipino restaurant (2015) was named the Washington Post's Restaurant of the Year by Tom Sietsema in 2023 — his highest annual honor. The Southern Foodways Alliance and Positively Filipino have both told its story; a diaspora home-away-from-home for kare-kare, crispy lechon kawali and lumpia.

dish: dim sum, beef chow fun, whole crispy fish, HK milk tea
address: 922 N St NW Rear, Washington, DC 20001
w: A playful Hong Kong-style Cantonese spot tucked in Shaw's Blagden Alley with red lanterns and night-market energy — dim sum, cheung fun, chow fun and whole crispy fish. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema ranked it #7 on his top-10 restaurants; Washingtonian and Time Out both praise it. Real Cantonese cooking inside the District.

dish: ajaruli & imeruli khachapuri, khinkali, pkhali
w: DC's first Georgian restaurant (Shaw, 2017), named for the Georgian celebratory feast, with a former Embassy of Georgia chef turning out molten-cheese khachapuri and soup-dumpling khinkali. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree; Washingtonian introduced it as the city's Georgian pioneer. A genuinely rare, city-unique cuisine.

dish: carrot wat, caramelized mushroom tibs, kay siga wat, yebeg wat
w: Yamrot Ezineh's farm-to-table Ethiopian kitchen in Columbia Heights, spices imported from Ethiopia, standout vegetable dishes (sweet-savory carrot wat, deeply caramelized mushroom tibs) alongside berbere beef and braised-lamb yebeg wat. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (2025) and to the Washington Post's best-Ethiopian roundup (2025).

dish: jollof rice, egusi, groundnut (peanut) soup, waakye, kenkey
w: Chef Prince Matey's home-cooked Ghanaian mainstay in Shaw (2015), which Eater calls "Shaw's essential Ghanaian mainstay" for its stellar groundnut soup, egusi and jollof; Washingtonian folded it into its guide to DC's West African cooking. Live bands on weekends and a diaspora crowd — authentic West African, not a fusion approximation.

dish: laksa, roti canai, nasi lemak, char kway teow
w: Chef James Wozniuk's Columbia Heights Malaysian restaurant (a Maketto and Spoken English alum) earned a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand in 2021 and won over DC's Malaysian community — Wozniuk even cooked for Malaysia's prime minister (DCist profiled the arc). CLOSED February 2025 amid neighborhood pressures; kept flagged as the notable Malaysian benchmark for the gap it leaves.

dish: dan dan noodles, Chengdu cold noodles, Shaanxi hand-pulled noodles, mapo tofu
address: 2700 New York Ave NE, Washington, DC 20002
w: The genuine-article Sichuan and Shaanxi kitchen hidden inside a Days Inn off New York Avenue NE. The Washington Post's $20 Diner said it "dazzles"; Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide calls it the best Chinese restaurant DC has ever had, with the best dan dan noodles the area has seen; Washington City Paper chronicled its cult following.

dish: doubles, dhalpuri & paratha roti, jerk wings, oxtail, fried snapper
w: Chef Peter Prime's small, bright H Street ode to Trinidad's Indian-African-Chinese street food — doubles, dhalpuri roti, jerk, oxtail and Caribbean rums. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree repeatedly (2020, 2024, 2025), a lone institutional authority; even Obama has been photographed eating a double there.

dish: tandoori lamb chops, black dal with burrata, wild-mushroom biryani
w: Rasika alums Suresh Sundas and Dante Datta's low-lit "Indian-ish" bar-restaurant off H Street — tandoori lamb chops, black dal moored with burrata, inventive cocktails. In the MICHELIN Guide (2022), on the New York Times' 50 Best New Restaurants in America, and a Washingtonian 100 Very Best pick; The Infatuation is a fan.

dish: twice-fried chicken, dumplings, num pang, Taiwanese noodles
w: Erik Bruner-Yang's genre-bending H Street Taiwanese-Cambodian restaurant, cafe and retail concept — dumplings, noodles and a cult twice-fried chicken. The Washington Post reviewed it as a party you can slurp, sip and shop through; The Infatuation calls the Taiwanese-Cambodian hybrid a standout. A rare Taiwanese anchor inside the District.

dish: doro wot, kitfo, vegetarian combo, injera
w: Ethiopian dining inside a classic Georgetown townhouse — soothing rooms, attentive service that walks newcomers through the menu, and a much-praised doro wot. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree (2021 onward), a lone institutional authority, and the rare authentic Ethiopian option west of the Little Ethiopia corridor.

dish: crispy duck, boat noodles, papaya salad, whole fish
w: The Columbia Pike Thai spot most beloved by the region's Thai community and "probably the one most popular with Thais." The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema put it in his Fall Dining Guide; Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide rates it among the three or four best Thai places around; ARLnow tracks its continued acclaim. Authentic, not Americanized.
